notes.meaning: A man named Lazarus fell severely ill in the village of Bethany, where he lived with his sisters Mary and Martha. Bethany was a small town located just east of Jerusalem across the Mount of Olives. John introduces this family because Jesus was about to perform one of His greatest signs there.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars have suggested that Lazarus of Bethany is linked to the poor beggar in Jesus' parable, or that the story grew out of that parable.

notes.meaning: John notes in advance that this Mary was the same woman who later poured expensive perfume on Jesus and wiped His feet with her hair. He mentions her famous act of devotion so his readers would easily recognize which family he was talking about. Her brother Lazarus was the one who had now become sick.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Western church tradition, following early thinkers like Augustine, historically identified this Mary of Bethany with the sinful woman who anointed Jesus in Luke 7.

notes.meaning: Mary and Martha sent an urgent message to Jesus explaining that the one He loved was sick. They did not demand that He come right away or tell Him what to do. They simply placed their deep need before Him, trusting His care for their brother.

Jesus told those listening that this illness would not end in final death. Instead, it would become an opportunity to display God's greatness and bring honor to the Son of God. Jesus knew Lazarus would die physically, but death would not have the last word.

John makes it clear that Jesus held a deep, personal affection for Martha, Mary, and Lazarus. When God delays His answers to our prayers, it is never because He has stopped loving us. His love remains steady even in the middle of family suffering.

Even after hearing that Lazarus was sick, Jesus stayed two more days where He was. He did not hurry because He moved entirely according to the Father's timetable. Waiting allowed circumstances to reach a point where God's power over death could shine most brightly.

After waiting two days, Jesus told His disciples it was time to head back to Judea. He was ready to leave the safe area east of the Jordan River to help His grieving friends. He walked toward danger because His love and duty called Him there.

The disciples were shocked by His decision because leaders in Judea had recently tried to stone Him to death. They could not understand why He would walk straight back into a place where His life was on the line. They feared both for His safety and for their own lives.

Jesus answered with a picture of a normal twelve-hour workday. A traveler walking in the daylight does not stumble because the sun lights the path. In the same way, Jesus was entirely safe as long as He walked within the time and purpose God had assigned to Him.

A person who walks in the dark will stumble because there is no light to guide the way. Jesus used this to show that real danger comes from acting outside God's will and timing. Walking away from God's guidance brings spiritual stumbling and harm.

Jesus told His followers that their friend Lazarus had fallen asleep and that He was going to wake him. In the Bible, sleep is a gentle way of describing death for believers because they will be raised again. Jesus spoke with complete authority, knowing He could wake the dead just like waking someone from a nap.

The disciples took His words literally and thought Lazarus had simply fallen into a restful sleep. In those days, sound sleep during a fever was taken as a healthy sign that the patient was getting better. They hoped this meant they would not need to make the dangerous trip to Judea.

The disciples thought Jesus was talking about natural rest, but He was actually using a word picture for death. They easily got confused by spiritual terms and missed what He was saying. John points out their misunderstanding to show how human thinking often falls short of God's meaning.

Seeing their confusion, Jesus dropped the figure of speech and told them directly that Lazarus was dead. He knew this through His divine knowledge, even though no human messenger had arrived with the news. He spoke plainly so they would face the reality of what had happened.

Jesus told them He was glad He had not been there to heal Lazarus, because what was coming would strengthen their faith. Raising a dead man after several days would be a far greater proof of God's power than healing a sick friend. Then He called them to go with Him to Lazarus.

Thomas, whose Greek name Didymus meant twin, spoke up to the other disciples. He expected that going to Judea would lead to their execution alongside Jesus. Even though his outlook was gloomy, his loyalty was fierce enough that he chose to die with his Master rather than leave Him.

When Jesus finally arrived near Bethany, Lazarus had already been buried in a tomb for four full days. Jewish families buried their dead on the very day of death, so there was no mistaking that he was gone. This four-day delay proved beyond any doubt that what would happen was a real miracle, not a temporary recovery.

Bethany sat less than two miles east of Jerusalem, just across the Mount of Olives. Because the village was so close to the main city, news traveled quickly between them. This short distance made it easy for many friends and religious leaders to visit the family.

Many Jewish people had come from Jerusalem to comfort Martha and Mary in their loss. Traditional mourning lasted for a full week, with visitors gathering to weep and offer sympathy. Their presence ensured that many witnesses would see the miracle Jesus was about to perform.

As soon as Martha heard that Jesus was on His way, she hurried outside the village to meet Him. Mary stayed sitting in the house, following the customary posture of deep grief. Martha's quick action reflected her practical, energetic nature.

Martha greeted Jesus with the honest ache of her heart, saying her brother would not have died if He had been there. She fully believed in His healing power and knew He could have saved Lazarus. Her words carried both a deep trust in Jesus and the natural sorrow of wondering what might have been.

Even in the midst of heartbreak, Martha declared that God would give Jesus whatever He asked. She still clung to faith in His special favor with God, even though her brother was already in the grave. Her prayer showed that her trust in Jesus survived the death of her brother.

differ.view: Some hold that Martha's words show she already believed Jesus had the power to raise Lazarus from the dead right then.
Others understand her words not as expecting Lazarus to be raised now, but as expressing lasting trust in Jesus despite not getting what she had hoped for.

notes.meaning: Jesus comforted Martha by assuring her that her brother would rise again. He stated this promise in general words to test and encourage her faith. While He meant an immediate resurrection, He spoke gently to lift her thoughts to God's ultimate power over death.

Martha replied that she already knew Lazarus would rise at the general resurrection on the last day. Most Jews of her day shared this belief, looking forward to the time at the end of history when God would raise the righteous. Yet this far-off hope did not bring much immediate relief to the grief she felt right then.

Jesus told Martha that He Himself is the resurrection and the life. Resurrection is not just a distant event on a calendar; it is a living reality found in Jesus. Anyone who puts their faith in Him will live forever, even if their physical body dies.

Jesus added that everyone who lives and believes in Him will never experience eternal death, which is final separation from God. Physical death cannot destroy the eternal life that Jesus gives to His people. He then looked directly at Martha and asked her if she truly believed this.

Martha answered with a clear and bold confession of faith. She stated that she believed He was the Christ (the promised Messiah) and the unique Son of God who was sent into the world. Even before seeing her brother raised, she placed her whole trust in who Jesus was.

After speaking with Jesus, Martha went back to the house and quietly called her sister Mary aside. She whispered the news so the crowd of mourners would not cause a disturbance or alert Jesus' enemies. She told Mary that the Teacher had arrived and was asking to see her.
